lessonTitle: Managing Chronic Pain: Treatments, Rehabilitation and Realistic Goals

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes cannot sleep because his feet burn and tingle as soon as he lies down. He has already tried paracetamol and ibuprofen without benefit and asks for something stronger. Managing chronic pain is less about finding the single right drug than about choosing the right class of treatment for the mechanism, and then agreeing realistic goals.

blocks.markdown: **Pharmacological options for neuropathic pain (objective 1).** Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system, such as painful diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia or radiculopathy. Simple analgesics and opioids work poorly. Drugs that reduce neuronal hyperexcitability or enhance descending inhibition are used instead. NICE guidance on neuropathic pain (check the current version) recommends offering one of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin as initial treatment for neuropathic pain other than trigeminal neuralgia, choosing according to comorbidity, risks, contraindications and preference. Carbamazepine is the first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia. Topical capsaicin cream may be considered for localised neuropathic pain in people who wish to avoid or cannot tolerate oral treatment. If the first drug fails or is not tolerated, another of the first-line drugs is tried; a drug is continued only if it gives meaningful benefit.

rows: Amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant)
Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition; sodium channel blockade
Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation), sedation, postural hypotension, cardiac conduction effects, toxicity in overdose
Duloxetine (SNRI)
Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, enhancing descending inhibition
Nausea, dizziness, raised blood pressure, sexual dysfunction; discontinuation symptoms
Gabapentin and pregabalin (gabapentinoids)
Bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing release of excitatory transmitters
Sedation, dizziness, peripheral oedema, weight gain, respiratory depression with opioids, misuse potential (controlled drugs in the UK); dose reduction in renal impairment
Carbamazepine
Sodium channel blockade
First-line in trigeminal neuralgia; drowsiness, hyponatraemia, rash, drug interactions; HLA-related and haematological risks
Topical capsaicin or lidocaine
Capsaicin depletes substance P and desensitises nociceptors; lidocaine blocks sodium channels
Local burning after capsaicin; few systemic effects
blocks.caption: First-line neuropathic pain drugs and key cautions. Start low, titrate slowly and review; Check against current BNF and local guidance.
NNT is the number needed to treat for one additional patient to benefit; ARR is the absolute difference in the proportion of responders (as a decimal).

blocks.title: Interpreting a trial of a neuropathic pain drug
blocks.prompt: In a trial, 40% of patients taking a drug achieve at least 50% pain relief, compared with 22% on placebo. Calculate the number needed to treat and interpret it.

steps.text: Interpret: roughly six patients must be treated for one to gain at least 50% relief who would not have had it with placebo; most will not respond, which is why each trial of a drug needs a planned review and a stopping rule.

blocks.answer: NNT of about 6; most patients do not obtain a good response, so a review point and the willingness to stop or switch are essential.

blocks.markdown: **Physical, psychological and interventional treatment (objective 2).** For chronic pain, treatment aims to improve function, sleep, mood and quality of life; pain intensity falls, if at all, modestly. *Physical* approaches include graded activity and exercise programmes, physiotherapy, pacing and, where appropriate, manual therapy. NICE guidance on chronic primary pain (check the current version) recommends supervised exercise and psychological therapy, and an antidepressant (such as amitriptyline, duloxetine or an SSRI) rather than opioids, gabapentinoids or NSAIDs. *Psychological* therapies, notably cognitive behavioural therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy, target catastrophising, fear-avoidance and sleep problems. *Interventional* techniques (nerve root and joint injections, radiofrequency treatments, nerve blocks, spinal cord stimulation) are considered selectively, usually in a specialist service, for defined conditions and as part of a rehabilitation plan. They carry procedural risk and the benefit is often short-lived.

rows: Physical
Graded exercise, pacing, physiotherapy
Improves function, mood and sleep; needs regular participation and reinforcement
Psychological
CBT, acceptance and commitment therapy, pain management programmes
Reduces distress and disability; skills based; works with patient expectation
Pharmacological
Antidepressants, gabapentinoids, topical agents
Modest average effect; trial with review and stopping rule
Interventional
Epidural or nerve root steroid injection, radiofrequency, spinal cord stimulation
Selected patients, usually short-term relief; adjunct to rehabilitation; procedural risk
blocks.caption: Treatment modalities for chronic pain and their roles.

blocks.title: Setting a function-based goal and checking progress
blocks.prompt: A patient with chronic neuropathic leg pain rates it 9/10 on a numerical rating scale and wants 'zero pain'. After 8 weeks of exercise and a titrated drug trial the score is 6/10, and she can walk 20 minutes instead of 5. How should progress be judged?

steps.text: Calculate the percentage change in pain intensity.
Compare with the agreed goal. A reduction of about 30% is often regarded as clinically meaningful (a rough guide, not a rule), and walking time has quadrupled.

Conclude that the treatment is working in terms of function, even though pain is far from zero; continue, and reset goals (for example walking to the shops), rather than stopping the plan or escalating to opioids.

blocks.answer: About 33% pain reduction with a large functional gain: a meaningful success; goals are reset rather than aiming for zero pain.

blocks.markdown: **Setting realistic goals and managing expectations (objective 3).** Chronic pain is usually managed, not cured. Begin by exploring what the patient hopes for and what they fear, then agree goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-limited (SMART) and based on function (for example returning to a hobby or sleeping through the night). Explain the mechanism in simple terms and that pain is real even when imaging is reassuring. Agree a trial of each treatment with a review date and a stopping rule. Use validated tools for pain, function, mood and sleep. Say that treatment is shared, and what the patient can do, such as activity pacing and sleep routines.

items: Acknowledge the pain and its impact before explaining limits.
Explore expectations and fears; agree that cure is unlikely but improvement is achievable.
Set two or three SMART, function-based goals.
Explain each treatment's likely benefit (for example the NNT) and risks, and agree a review date and stopping rule.
Plan self-management: exercise, pacing, sleep and mood; arrange psychological support and a rehabilitation programme.
Document the plan and avoid escalating drug doses in the absence of benefit.

blocks.title: Opioids and gabapentinoids
blocks.text: Opioids are not recommended as a first-line option for neuropathic or chronic primary pain: benefit is limited and harms (tolerance, dependence, overdose, hyperalgesia) are substantial; if started, they are a time-limited trial with review. Gabapentinoids carry a risk of misuse and respiratory depression, especially with opioids, and are controlled drugs in the UK. Check against current BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: Treat the mechanism and the person
blocks.text: Match drugs to the pain mechanism, give each a trial with review, add exercise and psychological therapy, reserve interventional techniques for selected patients, and anchor everything to goals that the patient values.

points: First-line neuropathic pain drugs are amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin; carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia and topical capsaicin for localised pain.
NNT converts trial results into how many patients must be treated for one extra responder; most patients do not respond to any single drug, so trials need review.
Exercise, psychological therapy and selected interventional procedures complement drugs, and chronic primary pain guidance avoids opioids and NSAIDs.
Goals should be realistic, function-based and reviewed; the aim is better living with pain rather than cure. Check drugs against the BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has severe paroxysmal electric shock-like facial pain triggered by chewing and washing her face. Which drug is the first-line choice recommended in NICE-style guidance?

distractorRationale.a: Amitriptyline is first-line for other neuropathic pain, not for trigeminal neuralgia.
distractorRationale.b: Opioids are not recommended first-line for neuropathic pain.
distractorRationale.c: Anti-inflammatory drugs do not target the neuropathic mechanism.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.explanation: The paroxysmal, trigger-evoked unilateral facial pain describes trigeminal neuralgia, which responds to sodium channel blockade. Carbamazepine is used first, with monitoring for sodium, rash and interactions; the BNF and local guidance should be checked.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has postherpetic neuralgia. He has benign prostatic hyperplasia with a past episode of urinary retention. Which first-line drug is the most concerning choice for him?

options.text: Gabapentin with dose adjustment for renal function

distractorRationale.a: Topical capsaicin has local burning but no urinary effect.
distractorRationale.b: Topical lidocaine has minimal systemic effects.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: its anticholinergic effects can precipitate urinary retention.
distractorRationale.d: Gabapentin is acceptable with renal dose adjustment and care about sedation.

questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants block muscarinic receptors, so urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth and confusion are particular risks in older men with prostatic obstruction. Alternatives with fewer anticholinergic effects are preferred.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has had low back pain for two years with no red flags and normal imaging. Which treatment is most appropriate to offer?

options.text: A supervised exercise programme with psychological therapy

questions.correctOptionText: A supervised exercise programme with psychological therapy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: exercise and psychological approaches improve function and are recommended.
distractorRationale.c: Strong opioids are not recommended for chronic primary pain.
distractorRationale.d: Injections give limited and short-lived benefit and should not be used alone.

questions.explanation: Chronic pain responds best to a rehabilitative approach that restores activity, treats distress and sleep problems, and builds self-management. Drugs and procedures are adjuncts rather than the main treatment.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of interventional procedures in chronic pain?

options.text: They replace the need for psychological therapy
They are considered for selected patients, usually within a rehabilitation plan, and benefit is often temporary
They are the first-line treatment for all chronic pain
They are risk-free and provide permanent cure

questions.correctOptionText: They are considered for selected patients, usually within a rehabilitation plan, and benefit is often temporary

distractorRationale.b: Correct: selected, adjunctive and usually time-limited benefit.
distractorRationale.d: Procedures carry risks and rarely cure.

questions.explanation: Injections and radiofrequency procedures may allow a patient to engage in exercise and rehabilitation, but they are not curative. Decisions should be taken within a specialist pain service with a clear aim and a review.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a SMART goal for a patient with chronic pain?

options.text: Walk to the end of my road and back with the dog three times a week within six weeks

questions.correctOptionText: Walk to the end of my road and back with the dog three times a week within six weeks

distractorRationale.c: Correct: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-limited.
distractorRationale.d: Not realistic or measurable as chronic pain rarely resolves completely.

questions.explanation: A SMART goal defines an activity, a frequency and a time-frame so progress can be reviewed. Function-based goals keep the patient focused on what matters to them rather than on a pain score alone.

questions.stem: Opioids are recommended as the first-line drug treatment for neuropathic pain.
questions.explanation: Opioids have limited benefit in neuropathic pain, and carry risks including tolerance, dependence and respiratory depression. First-line drugs are amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin (carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia); check current guidance.

questions.stem: In a trial of a drug for painful neuropathy, 45% of treated patients achieve at least 50% pain relief, compared with 25% on placebo. Calculate the number needed to treat (NNT), as a whole number of patients.
questions.explanation: The absolute difference in responders is 0.45 - 0.25 = 0.20. The NNT is the reciprocal, 1 / 0.20 = 5, meaning five patients are treated for one additional responder.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic pain rates it 8/10 before treatment and 5/10 after a 12-week programme. Calculate the percentage reduction in the pain score.
questions.explanation: The fall in score is 8 - 5 = 3 points. Dividing by the starting score gives 3 / 8 = 0.375, which is 37.5%. A reduction of about 30% is often regarded as meaningful, but function and mood should be judged alongside the score.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man has burning pain and allodynia in the groin and upper thigh three months after an inguinal hernia repair. Simple analgesics have not helped. Outline a stepwise management plan covering drugs, physical and psychological treatment and interventional options.
markingGuide: First-line drug (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin) chosen by comorbidity, started low and titrated slowly
Topical capsaicin or lidocaine as options; avoid opioids
Time-limited trial with review and stopping rule; try an alternative first-line drug if ineffective
Graded activity, physiotherapy, pacing and sleep measures
Psychological support (CBT or acceptance and commitment therapy) if distress or avoidance
Referral to specialist pain service for nerve block or other interventional options if unresponsive
Check doses against BNF and local guidance
questions.explanation: A structured plan matches treatment to the mechanism, includes non-drug measures and specialist input, and uses reviews to prevent endless dose escalation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with chronic pain asks for a stronger opioid and says she expects to be pain free. Describe how you would respond to set realistic goals and manage her expectations.
markingGuide: Acknowledge and validate the pain; explore expectations and fears
Explain that chronic pain is usually managed rather than cured, and why opioids have limited benefit and real harms
Agree two or three SMART function-based goals
Offer alternatives: exercise, psychological therapy, a drug trial with review and stopping rule
Agree outcome measures and a review date
Shared decision making, self-management plan and safety-netting; document
questions.explanation: Expectations are shaped by honest explanation and shared goals. Offering an active plan avoids the sense of being dismissed when opioids are declined.
